amstar2_items.justification: Research questions and eligibility criteria define the geographic setting (Kathmandu Valley, Nepal) and three broad thematic domains (water contamination, public health risks, and governance), but do not specify structured PICO/PECO populations, exposures/interventions, comparators, or study design criteria.

Critical flaw: Section 2.1 explicitly reports that the review was retrospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/w94yr/) only during the manuscript revision process in June 2026, nearly a year after the July 2025 search; no prospective protocol existed prior to conducting the review.

Sections 2.1, 2.3, and 2.7 explain the inclusion of heterogeneous quantitative, qualitative, and selected institutional grey literature designs (while excluding editorials and opinion commentaries) as necessary to capture the multidisciplinary environmental, epidemiological, household, and governance dimensions of urban water insecurity.

Critical flaw: Although five databases (PubMed, ProQuest, SpringerLink, Google Scholar, NepJOL) and grey literature portals were searched with example Boolean keyword pairs, no full database-specific search strings are provided, English-language and 2000-2025 restrictions are not justified, reference lists and experts were not consulted, and retrieving only 70 total records across five databases (including Google Scholar) over a 25-year window indicates a severely incomplete search execution.
No independent duplicate screening is reported in Section 2.4, and the Author Contributions statement attributes investigation, data curation, and formal analysis solely to the first author (G.B.B.).

Section 2.5 mentions a standardized extraction matrix, but does not report duplicate independent data extraction or verification by a second reviewer, and Author Contributions lists only G.B.B. for investigation and data curation.

Critical flaw: Section 2.4 and Figure 1 report aggregate counts and general reasons for the 10 full-text exclusions, but no bibliography or supplementary list identifying the 10 excluded full-text articles is provided.

No study-by-study characteristics table is provided; Table 1 explicitly presents only a domain-level summary rather than an individual study inventory, omitting study-specific designs, sample sizes, settings, and outcomes, and failing even to cite all 45 purportedly included sources in Results.
Critical flaw: Section 2.7 explicitly states that a formal standardized quality appraisal or risk-of-bias tool was not applied to the included studies.
The review does not report or discuss funding sources for any of the included primary or grey literature studies.
No quantitative meta-analysis was performed; the authors synthesized findings narratively across thematic domains due to study heterogeneity.

Critical flaw: Because no formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed, study quality is not systematically accounted for when interpreting findings; advocacy/media blog posts (e.g., Earth.Org, Think Global Health, We Are Water Foundation, The Water Project) and secondary reviews are synthesized alongside empirical laboratory and household datasets without quality differentiation.

Sections 3.2, 3.3, 4.1, and 4.6 discuss spatial, hydrogeological (shallow vs. deep aquifers), altitudinal, seasonal (monsoon vs. dry season), socio-economic, and methodological sources of variation across included studies.
No quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis was conducted.
Funding (no external funding), NSF IRES program acknowledgments, and conflicts of interest (none declared) are explicitly reported on page 17.

raw_response.methodological_notes: 1. Design vs. execution: Although self-described as a PRISMA 2020 systematic review with OSF registration, registration was performed retrospectively during peer-review revision (June 2026), no risk-of-bias/quality tool was applied, only 70 total records were retrieved across 5 databases (including Google Scholar) spanning 2000-2025, and findings are presented as an exploratory scoping/narrative thematic synthesis across environmental contamination (28 studies), public health/AMR (10), household coping (5), seasonal surface water (7), and governance (8). 2. Narrow Criterion 2 audit: Governance and regulatory gaps form one of the review's three explicit research questions (RQ3; Section 3.5; Section 4.3), covering overlapping agency mandates, weak regulatory oversight of informal tanker markets/private water vendors (Sapkota 2014 [28]), and groundwater transition from open-access to state-regulated resource (Pandey & Kazama 2023 [33]). However, legal/tenure/tariff/regulatory mechanisms are treated only as high-level descriptive themes secondary to biophysical water contamination monitoring, justifying 'borderline_narrow_c2'. 3. Included-studies accounting anomaly: The paper reports 45 included studies, provides no study-by-study table or supplement (Table 1 explicitly gives only 'Representative Studies' by domain), and lists only 49 total references in the entire bibliography. Subtracting 5 non-Nepal conceptual/guideline references ([34] Jepson 2017, [35] Wutich 2017, [36] Balazs & Ray 2014, [37] Page 2021 PRISMA, [45] Suraifi 2023) leaves 44 Nepal/Kathmandu references in total: 38 cited in Table 1/Results (extracted above; note [29] is itself a review and [5, 21, 30, 32] are online media/NGO pages) plus 6 cited only in Introduction or Discussion ([11] Khatiwada 2002, [44] Khare 2025, [46] Katuwal 2012 PhD thesis, [47] Shrestha 2023 review, [48] Chattopadhyay 2025 scoping review, and [49] Shrestha et al. 2024 IWMI blog—notably the only IWMI source matching Section 2.2's search description), while conceptual paper [36] (Balazs & Ray 2014) is erroneously cited in Table 1 under 'Representative Studies' (38 + 6 + [36] = 45). No literal DOI strings are printed in the Reference list (only '[CrossRef]' links).
